title: Inside a cell: the power stations, the recipe book and the workshops

summary.text: A cube of beetroot stays pale in cold water. Dropped in hot water, it spills red in minutes. The red was locked inside the cells all the time. In this unit your child finds the small rooms inside a cell and what each one does. They test what keeps the red in, pull stringy DNA out of a banana, and see how a recipe is copied and built into a protein. They learn why a cell with the same recipe book as every other cell still becomes muscle or skin, and why two of the rooms were once free-living bacteria.
summary.art: A beetroot cube in a clear glass of hot water, with red colour streaming out of it, next to a second glass of cold water that stays clear.

intro.hook: Run on the spot for one minute, then put a hand on your chest. Your heart is thumping and you are breathing hard. You also feel warm.
intro.text: Nothing in your body is a fire. Yet you got warm, and you needed more air. The answer is inside your cells. Each cell is full of small rooms, and some of them turn food and air into the energy you just used. In this unit you open the cell and look at the rooms, one by one.
intro.art: A child with a hand on their chest after running, and beside them a zoomed-in muscle cell full of small bean-shaped rooms.

outcomes: I can name the main rooms of a cell (organelles) and say what each one does.
I can explain how a cell copies a recipe from her DNA and builds a protein from it.
I can explain how mitochondria turn food and oxygen into energy, and why a hard-working cell has many.
I can run a fair test on beetroot and explain why heat and soap make the red spill out.
I can explain that the nucleus keeps the recipes but a cell reads different pages in different jobs.
I can give three pieces of evidence that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria.
I can say where the city picture of a cell helps and where it misleads.
I can name some things nobody knows yet about how cells work and how they began.

terms.meaning: A small room inside a cell that does one job. The word means 'little organ'.
terms.example: The nucleus, the mitochondria and the ribosomes are organelles.
terms.art: A cut-open cell with five small rooms, each a different shape and colour.

terms.meaning: The round room in many cells where the DNA is kept. It has a skin with tiny doors in it.
terms.example: Your cheek cells each have one nucleus about 6 micrometres across.
terms.art: A cell with a large round nucleus, its double skin with small pores, and threads of DNA inside.

terms.meaning: A very long thread of four kinds of chemical letters. The order of the letters is a set of recipes.
terms.example: The DNA in one human cell is about two metres long when stretched out.
terms.art: A long twisted ladder with four colours of rungs, wound into a tiny ball.

terms.meaning: One recipe on the DNA. Most genes tell the cell how to build one protein.
terms.example: A gene tells your cells how to make the protein that carries oxygen in red blood.
terms.art: A short stretch of a DNA thread marked off in a bright colour.

terms.meaning: A chain of small building blocks (amino acids), folded into a shape. Proteins do most of the work in a cell.
terms.example: The stretchy part of your muscle and the digestive juices in your stomach are proteins.
terms.art: A folded ribbon of coloured beads in a lumpy shape.

terms.meaning: A short working copy of one gene. It leaves the nucleus and carries the recipe to the ribosomes.
terms.example: Think of a photocopy of one recipe page, taken out of the library while the book stays inside.
terms.art: A short strand leaving a nucleus through a pore and travelling to a small ribosome.

terms.meaning: A tiny machine that reads a messenger copy and builds a protein from it. A cell has millions.
terms.example: A ribosome in a bacterium adds about 20 building blocks to a protein every second.
terms.art: A two-part tiny machine sliding along a strand while a chain of beads grows out of it.

terms.meaning: A bean-shaped room that releases energy from food, using oxygen. More than one are called mitochondria.
terms.example: A heart muscle cell is packed with thousands of mitochondria.
terms.art: A bean-shaped room with a double skin and a wavy folded inner wall.

terms.meaning: A small molecule that carries energy to where a cell needs it. It is used almost as fast as it is made.
terms.example: Every time a muscle cell pulls, it spends ATP.
terms.art: A small battery-shaped molecule moving from a mitochondrion to a muscle thread.

terms.meaning: The steps by which a cell uses oxygen to release energy from sugar. It makes carbon dioxide, water and ATP. It is not the same as breathing, but breathing brings the oxygen.
terms.example: The carbon dioxide you breathe out was made by your cells during respiration.
terms.art: Sugar and oxygen going into a mitochondrion, and carbon dioxide, water and small energy packets coming out.

terms.meaning: A green room in plant cells that catches sunlight and uses the light to make sugar. It has its own small piece of DNA.
terms.example: Each cell of a spinach leaf holds many chloroplasts.
terms.art: A green oval room with stacks of flat green discs inside.

terms.meaning: A stack of flat bags that sorts, labels and posts finished proteins to where they are needed.
terms.example: Proteins that your cells send out as digestive juice pass through the Golgi first.
terms.art: A stack of flat curved bags with small bubbles leaving one side.

terms.meaning: A small bag of strong digestive juice. It breaks down old parts and swallowed germs.
terms.example: A white blood cell that swallows a germ breaks the germ down in lysosomes.
terms.art: A small round bag with a germ being broken into pieces inside.

terms.meaning: A bag in a cell that stores water and other things. In a plant cell, one big vacuole fills most of the cell.
terms.example: The red colour in a beetroot is stored in the big vacuoles of its cells.
terms.art: A plant cell mostly filled by one big pale-red bag, with the other rooms squeezed to the sides.

terms.meaning: One long piece of DNA wound up with proteins. Humans have 46 in most cells.
terms.example: You got 23 chromosomes from your mother's egg and 23 from your father's sperm.
terms.art: A single X-shaped rod, with a long thread unwinding from one end.

terms.meaning: Living inside another being, and both of them gaining. Mitochondria and chloroplasts began this way.
terms.example: The bacteria that moved into a larger cell about two billion years ago became mitochondria.
terms.art: A large cell with a smaller bacterium inside her, the two joined by a thin line.

explanations.concept: A cell is a crowded city of small rooms
explanations.definition: Most cells of plants, animals and fungi hold organelles: small rooms, each wrapped in its own skin, each with its own job.
explanations.description: In Class 4 you met the three main parts of a cell, the membrane, the cytoplasm and the nucleus. Now we go inside the cytoplasm. It is not empty jelly. It is full of organelles, packed close together, like shops and workshops along a busy street. Having separate rooms lets a cell do many jobs at once without mixing them up. The digestive juice sits in a bag of its own, so it does not eat the rest of the cell. Bacteria are smaller and have no rooms wrapped in skins. Their DNA floats in the cytoplasm, and they still have ribosomes. A city is a good picture for the rooms. It is a poor picture in one way. A real cell is not a still map. Everything in her moves, bumps and changes all the time.
examples: A liver cell has a nucleus, a thousand or more mitochondria, ribosomes, and rooms for sorting and recycling.
A bacterium has a membrane, cytoplasm, a loop of DNA and ribosomes, but no rooms wrapped in skins.
A red blood cell has lost her nucleus and most of her rooms so she can carry more oxygen.
explanations.art: A cut-open cell drawn like a bird's-eye map of a city, with each room as a small building.

explanations.concept: The nucleus: a library, not a boss
explanations.definition: The nucleus is a room with a double skin that holds the cell's DNA, wound into chromosomes. It makes working copies of genes and sends them out.
explanations.description: Your DNA is about two metres long in each cell. It is folded to fit in a nucleus about six micrometres wide. That is like packing a thread 20 kilometres long into a tennis ball. The nucleus has tiny doors called pores. Copies of single genes go out through the pores, and the DNA itself stays in. Many books call the nucleus the control centre. That picture is useful, but it can mislead. The nucleus does not give orders on her own. Signals from the rest of the cell and from outside her tell the nucleus which genes to copy. In the 1930s and 1940s, a German scientist named Joachim Hammerling cut up Acetabularia, a giant single-celled alga that grows several centimetres tall. A stalk with no nucleus could grow one new cap, using messages already sent out, but not a second one. When he joined a stalk of one species to a foot of another, the new cap came to match the species of the nucleus. So the nucleus matters a great deal. But the messages, the stalk and the whole cell matter too.
examples: A human cell has 46 chromosomes in the nucleus, which hold about 20,000 genes that make proteins.
A mature red blood cell has no nucleus and still lives about four months.
In Acetabularia, a stalk with no nucleus can still grow one cap, from messages already sent out.
explanations.art: A nucleus with a double skin and pores, DNA threads inside, and arrows showing copies of single genes going out and signals coming in.

explanations.concept: From recipe to protein: copy, carry, build
explanations.definition: A cell builds a protein in three steps. She copies a gene into messenger RNA, the copy travels to a ribosome, and the ribosome builds the protein from it.
explanations.description: DNA is written with four letters. A ribosome reads the copy three letters at a time, and each three-letter word means one building block. It adds the blocks in order. The chain folds up into a protein with its own shape. The shape decides the job. Change one letter in a gene, and one block can change, and the shape can change. Sometimes nothing changes, because several different words mean the same block. Sometimes one changed block makes a protein that does its job badly. Ribosomes are so small that their shape was found only in the year 2000. Ada Yonath, Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and Thomas Steitz each solved it, and they shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Ramakrishnan grew up in Tamil Nadu. Yonath started working on ribosomes in the 1970s, when many scientists said the work was impossible.
examples: The gene for the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood is copied again and again in young red blood cells.
A sickle-shaped red blood cell comes from one changed letter that changes one block in the protein.
Some antibiotics work by blocking bacterial ribosomes and leaving ours alone.
explanations.art: A DNA strand, a short messenger copy, and a ribosome building a chain of coloured beads, in three panels.

explanations.concept: Folding, labelling and posting: rough ER and Golgi
explanations.definition: Many proteins pass through the rough endoplasmic reticulum (rough ER), where they are folded, and then the Golgi body, where they are labelled and sent on.
explanations.description: Some ribosomes float free in the cytoplasm. Others sit on a maze of flat folded bags called the rough ER, and the protein they build is fed inside the bag as it grows. There it is folded and checked. Little bubbles then carry it to the Golgi body, a stack of flat bags. The Golgi adds a label to each protein, like a postal address, and posts it. The protein may be sent to the membrane, to a lysosome, or out of the cell. Gland cells, which make digestive juices or milk, have a great deal of ER and Golgi. They are post offices working all day.
examples: Cells of the pancreas that make digestive juice are packed with rough ER.
Cells in the breast that make milk proteins have large Golgi bodies.
A cell can move a bubble along a track to the very edge of her membrane and release it.
explanations.art: A ribosome-covered folded bag next to a stack of flat bags, with small bubbles carrying proteins between them.

explanations.concept: Mitochondria: where food and oxygen become usable energy
explanations.definition: A mitochondrion has two skins. The inner skin is folded many times. On those folds, the cell uses oxygen to release energy from food and store it in ATP.
explanations.description: Cells need energy to move, build and pump. Food holds energy, but a cell cannot spend food directly. In the cytoplasm, a sugar is first split into two halves, without oxygen. This releases only a little energy. The halves then go into a mitochondrion. There, with oxygen, the cell releases about fifteen times more. The energy is packed into small carriers called ATP. The folds make a large surface, so there is room for many tiny machines to work. The cell breathes out carbon dioxide and makes water. ATP is spent almost as fast as it is made. A resting adult makes and uses about their own body weight in ATP in a day, but holds less than a hundred grams at any moment. So a cell must keep making it, and stops within minutes without oxygen. Some of the energy leaves as heat, and that is why you warm up when you run.
examples: A heart muscle cell has thousands of mitochondria, because she works every second of your life.
A mature red blood cell has none. She carries oxygen for others and does not use it herself.
The poison cyanide stops a mitochondrion from using oxygen, and the cell runs out of energy quickly.
explanations.art: A bean-shaped mitochondrion cut open to show the folded inner wall, with sugar and oxygen going in and ATP, carbon dioxide and water coming out.

explanations.concept: Chloroplasts: the sun-catching rooms that plants also need
explanations.definition: A chloroplast is a green room in plant and algae cells. It uses the energy of sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen.
explanations.description: Inside a chloroplast are stacks of flat discs, and the green chlorophyll sits on the discs. A leaf cell holds many chloroplasts, often 20 to 100. In the photosynthesis unit, leaf discs float because chloroplasts fill them with oxygen. Many children think plants have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria. That is wrong. Plants have both. The chloroplasts make sugar in the light. The mitochondria then release energy from that sugar, day and night, as they do in your cells. A plant is breathing all the time, and in the day she makes more oxygen than she uses.
examples: A spinach leaf cell has chloroplasts and mitochondria.
A root cell has mitochondria but no chloroplasts, because roots sit in the dark.
Some single-celled algae have one huge chloroplast shaped like a spiral ribbon.
explanations.art: A leaf cell with green chloroplasts and small bean-shaped mitochondria between them, and a big water vacuole to one side.

explanations.concept: Recycling, storage and the moving cell
explanations.definition: Lysosomes digest old parts and swallowed germs. Vacuoles store water and other things. Tracks inside the cell carry cargo from room to room.
explanations.description: A cell makes things and she also takes things apart. Lysosomes are small bags of strong juice that break down worn-out parts, so the building blocks can be used again. In 1955 a Belgian scientist named Christian de Duve found them. In 2016 a Japanese scientist named Yoshinori Ohsumi won the Nobel Prize for showing how a hungry cell eats her own old parts to survive. A plant cell keeps one big vacuole, which holds water, pigments and waste, and pushes the cell firm. Inside the cytoplasm there are also thin tracks made of protein. Tiny walking proteins carry bubbles along the tracks, a little like a person pulling a cart along a rope. In some water plants the whole cytoplasm streams round the cell, fast enough to see under a school microscope.
examples: Cells of your gut lining are replaced every few days, and their old parts are recycled.
A beetroot cell keeps its red pigment in its big vacuole.
A nerve cell can send bubbles along a track a metre long.
explanations.art: A cell with a lysosome digesting an old part, a big vacuole, and small walkers carrying bubbles along thin tracks.

explanations.concept: Two of the rooms were once bacteria
explanations.definition: Mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living bacteria that moved into larger cells long ago. Scientists call this endosymbiosis.
explanations.description: Both rooms have two skins, and both have their own small ring of DNA, like a bacterium. They make their own ribosomes, which are like bacterial ribosomes. They split in two to make more of themselves, and a cell cannot make one from nothing. Genetic tests of the ring of DNA show that mitochondria are closest to a family of bacteria and chloroplasts are closest to the blue-green bacteria. Over about two billion years, most of their genes moved to the nucleus, and today they cannot live alone. In most animals, the mitochondria in a baby come from the mother's egg. The father's sperm adds almost none. So you carry a line of mitochondria passed from your mother, her mother, and back through all the mothers of your family.
examples: Your mitochondria have their own ring of DNA, 16,569 letters long, with 37 genes.
Chloroplasts in a leaf cell have their own DNA ring, and some have been moved to the nucleus.
Antibiotics that hurt bacteria can also harm mitochondria in rare cases, as the two are alike.
explanations.art: A large cell with two smaller rooms drawn as bacteria that have settled inside, with dotted lines to free-living bacteria outside.

explanations.concept: How did the first complex cell begin?
explanations.definition: The first cell with a nucleus and mitochondria, called the first eukaryote, appeared about two billion years ago. How is still argued.
explanations.description: Everyone agrees mitochondria began as bacteria. The argument is about what came first. Some scientists think the host cell already had a nucleus and a way to swallow things, and she then swallowed a bacterium. Others think the host was an archaeon, a different kind of tiny cell, and the nucleus came later. Nick Lane, a British scientist, argues that the energy from the bacterium came first and made a large cell possible. In 2015 scientists found genes in deep-sea mud from a group called Asgard archaea that look like the genes of a cell with a nucleus, and many think they are the host's close cousins. Nobody has found a living cell in the middle of this change, so every route is still an idea.
examples: Asgard archaea found in deep-sea mud carry genes that eukaryotes also have.
A few single-celled parasites and gut dwellers have lost their mitochondria and kept only small remnants.
No living cell half-way between a bacterium and a eukaryote has been found.
explanations.art: A time line from simple cells to cells with a nucleus and mitochondria, with three arrows showing three routes scientists argue about.

perspectives.explanation: A larger cell already had a nucleus and could swallow things. She swallowed a bacterium that became the mitochondrion.
The bacterium moved in first and gave a cell the energy to grow large and keep a big library of genes. The nucleus followed.
The host was a close cousin of today's Asgard archaea, and she already had some genes that eukaryotes use.

explanations.concept: How does a cell choose which pages to read?
explanations.definition: All the cells in your body hold the same DNA, but a muscle cell, a nerve cell and a skin cell switch on different genes.
explanations.description: In 1962 a British scientist named John Gurdon took the nucleus from a tadpole's gut cell and moved the nucleus into a frog's egg whose own nucleus had been removed. Some of the eggs grew into tadpoles. So the gut cell's nucleus still held the whole recipe book. Gurdon and Shinya Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize for showing that a grown-up cell can start again. Cells choose pages using proteins called transcription factors, which attach to DNA and switch genes on or off. Chemical tags on the DNA also help. Signals from outside the cell, such as hormones and touch, change which switches are pressed. Scientists know many of the switches. They do not yet understand the whole pattern that makes a cell stay a muscle cell for decades.
examples: Muscle cells switch on genes for muscle proteins and keep the genes for skin proteins off.
Gurdon's frog nuclei showed the whole recipe stays in a grown-up cell.
Adult cells can be pushed back to an early state in a laboratory, and this is used to study disease.
explanations.art: Three cells with the same big book in the nucleus, each with a different page lit up in a different colour.

agreed.text: Cells of plants, animals and fungi contain organelles, small rooms wrapped in their own skins, each with its own job.
agreed.evidence: Electron microscopes, from the 1940s and 1950s onwards, showed the rooms. Scientists such as George Palade found their jobs by breaking cells apart and testing the pieces.

agreed.text: DNA holds the recipes, and a cell builds proteins by copying a gene into messenger RNA, which a ribosome reads.
agreed.evidence: The code was worked out in the 1960s by Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and others. Khorana, who was born in a village in Punjab in British India, shared the 1968 Nobel Prize for this.

agreed.text: Mitochondria release most of a cell's usable energy, using oxygen.
agreed.evidence: Mitochondria taken out of cells and given food and oxygen make ATP. The poison cyanide stops them using oxygen, and the cell runs out of energy.

agreed.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living bacteria.
agreed.evidence: They have their own ring-shaped DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes and two skins, and they divide on their own. Gene sequences from the 1970s and 1980s match them to bacteria.

agreed.text: Every cell in a body holds nearly the same DNA, yet cells of different jobs use different genes.
agreed.evidence: John Gurdon's 1962 frog experiment grew a whole tadpole from a gut cell's nucleus.

agreed.text: A fatty skin that is whole is needed for a cell to hold her contents in.
agreed.evidence: Beetroot cubes spill pigment when heat or soap breaks the skins of their cells.

challenging.claim: The nucleus is the brain or boss of the cell.
challenging.who: Many school books, which call the nucleus the control centre.
challenging.for: The nucleus holds the DNA, and a cell without a nucleus cannot grow or repair herself for long.
challenging.against: Mature red blood cells live for months with no nucleus. Mitochondria and chloroplasts keep their own DNA. Signals from outside the nucleus decide which genes are copied.

challenging.claim: Plants have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria.
challenging.who: Many children, and some older books.
challenging.for: Plants make their own food, so it seems they do not need to release energy.
challenging.against: Plant cells have both. Mitochondria release energy from the sugar that chloroplasts make, in the day and in the night.

challenging.for: Making ATP is their biggest job.
challenging.against: Mitochondria also help control calcium, make heat, make some building blocks, and start a cell's self-destruct programme when she is badly damaged.

challenging.claim: A cell is just a small factory that follows fixed instructions.
challenging.who: The machine picture in many books.
challenging.for: Parts do fixed jobs, and the DNA recipe is copied exactly.
challenging.against: A cell senses her surroundings, moves, repairs herself and changes which genes she uses. Several biologists, such as Denis Noble, argue that the whole cell, not only the DNA, shapes what happens.

big_questions.q: A muscle cell and a skin cell hold the same recipe book, and use different pages. What do you think decides which pages are read?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a muscle cell feels all day that a skin cell does not.

big_questions.q: Your mitochondria began as bacteria. Are they part of you, or are they guests who have stayed so long that they became family?
big_questions.hint: A mitochondrion cannot live alone now, and you cannot live without her.

big_questions.q: Every breath you take is for your cells. Where do you end and where do they begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air that went in this morning and the carbon dioxide that came out.

big_questions.q: A red blood cell has no nucleus and no recipe book, yet she does her job for four months. Is the recipe book part of being alive, or only part of making new cells?
big_questions.hint: Think of a cooked meal and a cookbook.

big_questions.q: The mitochondria in your cells came from your mother's egg, and hers from her mother. What do you think about a line of living beings passed down through only the mothers?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many lines of mothers lie behind you.

big_questions.q: A city has a mayor, but a cell has no single place that decides. If nobody is in charge, how does the cell act as one?
big_questions.hint: Think about a flock of birds turning together.

big_questions.q: A cell picture drawn in a book is flat and still. What did the drawing leave out, and does leaving it out change what you think a cell is?
big_questions.hint: Think of a photograph of a busy street.

big_questions.q: If the first complex cell was a team of two or more different beings, what does that tell you about how new kinds of life begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about joining, and not only about splitting.

story.title: The Song That Started Slowly
story.note: A made-up story. The people and the village race are imagined. The science in it is real: muscle cells keep a small store of ready energy, make more quickly but wastefully without oxygen, and reach their best supply only after a minute or two, when oxygen from the breath and blood reaches the mitochondria. Girls' and women's boat crews do race on the backwaters of Kerala today.
text: On the backwaters near Alappuzha, the long boat lay tied to a coconut palm. Twelve girls sat in it with their paddles across their knees, and every one of them was angry.

Meera stood in the middle of the boat with a wooden plank in her hand. She was ten, the youngest on the crew, and she was the singer. The girls rowed to her beat. When she sang fast, they pulled fast. That was the rule. In three weeks was the Onam race, and the girls from the next village had won it four years in a row.
'We lose at the second pole,' said Anitha, who sat at the back. 'Every time.'

It was true. Every practice, Meera's crew shot off the line like a fish. Her song was quick and bright. The paddles flashed, and the boat was ahead by the first pole. Then, somewhere before the second pole, the strokes grew ragged. Arms burned. Breath came in gasps. The boat from the next village slid past them, calm and steady, as if it had all the time in the world.

'You are not strong enough,' Anitha said to the girl in front of her. 'No, you are not fast enough,' said the girl. Soon everyone was saying something. Meera banged the plank on the side, and nobody heard her.

On the bank sat Kalyani Chechi on an upturned bucket, with a steel flask of tea. She was sixty-eight. When she was young, nobody in her village would let a girl near a racing boat, so she had rowed at night in a fishing canoe and learned by herself. She had watched every practice for two weeks and said nothing.
'Meera,' she called. 'Come here and put your hand on your chest.'
Meera climbed out. 'Now run to the coconut palm and back,' said Kalyani Chechi. Meera ran. When she came back, her heart was banging against her hand and her breath was loud.
'Good. Now tell me. When you started to run, how did you feel in the first ten steps?'
'Fine,' said Meera. 'Fast.'
'And at the end?'
'Tired. Like my chest was too small.'

'Your arms and legs are made of cells,' said Kalyani Chechi. 'My granddaughter showed me the word in her book. Every muscle cell has little rooms in her, called mitochondria. Those are the furnaces. They burn sugar from your food, but only with air. The air has to come in through your nose, go into your blood, and be carried to every cell. That takes time.'
'So what do the cells use at the start?'

'A small store of ready energy. It lasts a few seconds. Then they make more in a quick, wasteful way that needs no air, and it leaves an ache. Your furnaces need a minute or two to wake up and run properly. Until then, you are burning your matchsticks instead of your logs.'
Meera looked at the lake. At the first pole, her crew had been flying. At the second pole, they had run out of matchsticks.
'Your song starts too fast,' said Kalyani Chechi. 'You wake up the girls' arms before you wake up their furnaces.'

That evening, Meera tried a new song. It had the same words, but the beat was slow, like a heartbeat at rest. Pull. Breathe. Pull. Breathe. The girls grumbled. They said it felt like walking. But the boat did not tire at the second pole, and at the third pole Meera sang a little faster, and the crew went with her. They did not win the practice race. But for the first time, they did not fall back.

On the day of the race the lake was crowded and loud. Boats lay in a line. Meera held her plank. When the horn went, the boat from the next village shot ahead. Every girl behind Meera's back wanted to go with them. She could feel it in the boat, as if the water itself were pulling.
She began the slow song. 'Pull,' she sang. 'Breathe. Pull. Breathe.'
The other boat was two lengths ahead, and then three. People on the bank shouted. Anitha's paddle twitched. 'Not yet,' Meera sang, in the beat of the song. 'Not yet. Not yet.'

Past the first pole, she lifted the song a little. Past the second, she lifted it again. The next village's boat was rowing hard, and the strokes were growing short. Their paddles splashed. Meera's crew was breathing in time with her words, and every stroke came out long.

At the third pole, Meera sang as fast and bright as she had ever sung. And the girls answered. The boat leaned forward. Water hissed along the sides. The next village's boat came back, a length, then half a length, then it was beside them, and then it was behind.
They won by the nose of the boat.

Afterwards, the girls lay in the boat with their arms hanging over the sides, laughing and gasping. Meera sat with a hand on her chest. Her heart was thundering. She did not think of the race. She thought of the twelve girls, and of the millions of little furnaces in their arms, and how every one of them had been woken, slowly, on purpose, by a song.
story.epiphany: The girls had not run out of strength. They had started faster than the furnaces in their muscle cells could be fed with air. A slow start let the air catch up.
ask: Why did the slow song help the crew at the second pole, and not at the start?
What would you feel in your own arms if you sprinted at the start of a long walk?
Which part of a muscle cell was Kalyani Chechi calling the furnace, and what does it need?
Why is it better to speed up slowly in a long race?
