roots.context: We have looked inside the cell and found rooms, recipes and power stations. Now we ask what this says about who is in charge in a living thing, and about you.

deep_truth.truth: Your muscle cells and your skin cells hold the same recipe book in their nuclei. Yet each reads different pages, chosen by signals from outside the book. Mitochondria even keep a small recipe book of their own. So the nucleus stores the recipes, but it does not run the cell.
deep_truth.habit: We call the nucleus the control centre or the boss, as if a cell worked like an office with a manager. In a cell, the library and the work are in different rooms, and the whole cell, with signals from outside, decides which recipe to use.
deep_truth.evidence: In Gurdon's frog experiment, a gut cell's nucleus held the whole recipe for a tadpole. Muscle and skin cells use different pages from the same book. Mitochondria copy their own DNA, and red blood cells work for months with no nucleus.

three.who_am_i: You are about thirty trillion cells, and each one reads a different part of the same book. You are also a home for mitochondria, which began as bacteria and are passed down through your mother.
three.what_is_life: A living cell is a crowd of rooms, moving parts and signals that keep each other going. No single room is the whole of the cell.
three.what_is_this_world: The oxygen in your breath is carried to your mitochondria, and the carbon dioxide you breathe out is taken up by plants. Cells in leaves and cells in you are parts of one long exchange.

roots.thread: In a cell, no single part holds all the knowledge, and none gives all the orders. The recipe is in the nucleus, the energy is made in the mitochondria, and the building is done by ribosomes. These rooms depend on each other every second. Two of them began as separate beings and joined, so the cell herself is a meeting of many origins. The same is true of your whole body, and of the living world: parts that look separate keep each other alive. Where the working of a whole comes from is a question we leave open for you.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that if you strike the root, the middle or the top of a great tree, the tree bleeds but still lives, because life pervades the whole tree. When life leaves one branch, only that branch dries up.
teachings.link: The cell's life is also in every part, not in one control room. A red blood cell without a nucleus is still alive and working.

teachings.teaching: The best leader is one whom people hardly notice. When the work is done, the people say, 'We did it ourselves.'
teachings.link: A nucleus is a library and a source of copies, but the work is done everywhere in the cell, with no single boss.

teachings.teaching: Every jewel in a great net reflects every other jewel, so each one contains all the others.
teachings.link: Each part of a cell holds a piece of the same story. Mitochondria carry their own DNA, and the nucleus carries the rest.

science.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living bacteria that moved into larger cells about two billion years ago or more, and the cell has been a partnership ever since.
A cell may work as a whole system in which signals, rooms and DNA all shape each other, and DNA alone does not settle what a cell does.

other_view.who: Richard Dawkins and many gene-centred biologists
other_view.view: Genes are the main actors. A cell, and a body, is the machine that genes build to copy themselves. In this view, the nucleus really is the place where the most important information sits.

practice.title: Two minutes with your furnaces
practice.say: Sit still and put a hand on your chest. Breathe slowly for one minute and feel the air come in. Now run on the spot for twenty seconds. Sit down and notice your breath, your heartbeat and your warmth. Say quietly where the air is going.
practice.kid: Sit still. Put a hand on your chest. Breathe slowly. Now run on the spot for twenty seconds. Sit and notice your breath, your heart and your warmth. Where is the air going?

ask: If a cell has no single boss, how does she act as one?
Are the mitochondria in your cells you, or are they guests who have stayed?
If the same recipe book gives muscle and skin, what is the thing that makes the difference?
roots.art: A cell drawn as a lantern, with the nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes glowing in different colours and thin threads of light joining every room to every other.

games.title: Cell City Emergency: which room is it?
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card shows a problem in a cell. You pick the room that matters most and check the back.

setup.art: Twelve emergency cards in a pile in the middle of a table, with eight room tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards in a pile.

setup.art: One child reading an emergency card aloud while the others each push a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

setup.art: Tokens turned over together and the reader showing the answer on the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 12 two-sided cards: an emergency in the cell on the front, and the room that matters with the reason on the back

items.f: The food has arrived, but the cell has no way to turn it into usable energy. Which room is in trouble?
items.b: Mitochondria. They release energy from food with oxygen, and make ATP.

items.f: A heart muscle cell must work every second of your life. Which room will she have the most of?
items.b: Mitochondria. A heart muscle cell has thousands, to make the ATP that powers every beat.

items.f: A poison called cyanide stops the cell from using oxygen. Which room does it stop?
items.b: Mitochondria. They cannot finish releasing energy without oxygen, and the cell runs out of power quickly.

items.f: The master recipe book has been damaged by too much sunlight. Which room holds it?
items.b: The nucleus. It holds the DNA, so damage there can mean wrong recipes are copied.

items.f: A copy of a recipe has arrived at a workshop, but nobody is building the protein. Which room is missing?
items.b: Ribosomes. They read the messenger copy and build the protein.

items.f: A cell is making a lot of digestive juice, and the proteins are piling up unlabelled. Which room is slow?
items.b: The Golgi body. It labels and posts the proteins to where they are needed.

items.f: A poison has slipped into the cell through the gate. Which part should have kept it out?
items.b: The cell membrane. It lets some things through and keeps others out.

items.f: Sugar is waiting outside the cell and cannot get in by itself. Which part helps it in?
items.b: The cell membrane. Special proteins in it carry sugar across.

items.f: A white blood cell has swallowed a germ. Which room breaks the germ down?
items.b: The lysosome. It holds strong juices that digest the germ.

items.f: A leaf cell has been kept in a dark cupboard for a week. Which room cannot do its job?
items.b: The chloroplast. It needs light to make sugar.

items.f: A plant cell is wilting because her water store is empty. Which room is it?
items.b: The vacuole. In a plant cell, the big vacuole holds water and pushes the cell firm.

items.f: A copy of a gene is ready to leave the library, but the library stays closed. Which part holds the DNA and has tiny doors?
items.b: The nucleus. Its pores let copies out and keep the DNA inside.

printables.title: 8 room tokens: one set for each player (copy the sheet for every player)

rules: Each player has a set of eight room tokens.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player pushes one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader turns the card over and reads the room and the reason. A player with the right room scores two points.
A player with a wrong room scores one point if they can say in one sentence what that room really does.
The reader changes after each card. The player with the most points when the pile ends wins.
You can also play alone. Turn over a card, say your answer aloud, check the back, and count your right answers out of twelve.

No printer? Write each question and answer on a slip by hand, and write the eight room names on eight scraps for each player. Two players can also share one set of tokens and take turns. A grown-up helps younger children with the scissors.

flow.do: Cut out the twelve cards and the eight room tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player a set of tokens.
flow.say: These cards show a problem in a cell. You pick the room that matters. Each player has eight tokens. Let us look at them once.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take a set of tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cell City Emergency. You set up the cards and tokens.

flow.do: Play the first four cards. After each, ask why the wrong rooms would not fit.
flow.say: Reader, read the card. Everyone, push a token. Why that room?
flow.kid: Play four cards. Say why you picked each room.

ask.q: Why does the heart muscle cell need so many mitochondria?
good: She works all the time and needs lots of energy.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first four cards.

flow.do: Play the next four cards. Ask the reader to say what the room does, not just its name.
flow.say: Next four. After the answer, say what the room does in your own words.
flow.kid: Play four more cards. After each, say what the room does.
flow.context: In this step, you play the middle four cards.

flow.do: Play the last four cards. Count the points. Ask which card was the hardest and why.
flow.say: Last four. Count your points. Which card was the trickiest?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points. Which card was trickiest?
flow.context: This is the last step of Cell City Emergency. You finish the pile and count the points.

experiments.title: The Beetroot Test: what keeps the red inside the cells?
experiments.question: Does the red of a beetroot stay inside its cells in cold water, in warm water, in hot water, and in soapy water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which glass will turn the reddest, and which will stay clear? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every glass gets the same amount of water, two cubes of the same size, and the same 20 minutes. Only one thing changes between glasses: cold, warm, hot, or cold with soap. All the cubes are rinsed first, so the red you see comes from inside the cells.
results_table: Colour of the cube at the end

materials.item: 1 fresh raw beetroot, firm
4 clear glasses or small clear jars, the same size (thick glass or jam jars, because thin glass can crack with boiling water)
a sharp knife and a chopping board (for the grown-up)
a kettle, or a pan of water just boiled (for the grown-up)
1 teaspoon of liquid dish soap
a teaspoon, a bowl of cold water and a spoon for lifting cubes
a sheet of white paper to hold behind the glasses
a timer or a phone clock
a pencil and a marker for labelling the glasses
a thermometer, if you have one (optional)

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the beetroot and pours the hot water. The hot glass stays on the tray, away from the edge. Beetroot juice stains hands and clothes, so wear an old shirt. Do not drink the water from any glass. Nobody touches glass C until it has cooled.
experiments.record: Write a colour score for each glass at 5, 10 and 20 minutes: 0 for clear, 1 for the faintest pink, 3 for clearly pink, 5 for deep red. Write the colour of the cube at the end. Then draw the four glasses with the colours you saw.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out what keeps the red colour inside a beetroot. You use cold, warm and hot water, and soap.

setup.art: Four clear glasses labelled A, B, C and D in a row on a tray, each with about half a cup of liquid and a label.
setup.caption: 1. Set out four glasses. A is cold, B is warm, C is hot and D is cold with soap.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting a beetroot into small cubes about as wide as a fingertip on a chopping board.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts the beetroot into cubes the size of a fingertip.

setup.art: Beetroot cubes being rinsed in a bowl of cold water until the water stays almost clear.
setup.caption: 3. Rinse all the cubes in cold water, until the rinse water is almost clear.

setup.art: A hand dropping two cubes into each of the four glasses at the same time, with a timer beside them.
setup.caption: 4. Drop two cubes into each glass at the same moment. Start the timer.

setup.art: The four glasses held in front of a white paper, showing four different shades from clear to deep red.
setup.caption: 5. After 20 minutes, hold each glass in front of white paper and score its colour.

flow.do: Set out four glasses and label them A, B, C and D. Read out what each will hold. Ask for a guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will test four glasses. A has cold water. B has warm water. C has hot water. D has cold water with soap. Which will turn reddest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four glasses. A is cold. B is warm. C is hot. D has soap. Which turns reddest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that glass will be the reddest?
good: The hot water will pull the colour out.
Heat is stronger than cold.
Soap cleans the colour off.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the results table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Beetroot Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the beetroot into eight cubes, each about one centimetre wide. Put the cubes in a bowl of cold water for two minutes. Change the water until it stays almost clear.
flow.say: A grown-up will cut the cubes. Cut cells leak red at the cut edge. We rinse them first, so only the red from inside the whole cells is left to test.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts eight cubes. Rinse them in cold water until it stays almost clear.
flow.parent: If the rinse water keeps turning red, change it two or three times. This washes off the red from the broken cells at the cut surface. Use fresh, firm raw beetroot. Cooked beetroot has dead cells and gives a muddy result.
flow.context: This step prepares the beetroot cubes, so the test is fair.

flow.do: Pour about half a cup of water into each glass. A gets cold tap water. B gets warm water that feels hand-hot. C gets water just off the kettle, poured by a grown-up. D gets cold tap water and a teaspoon of dish soap, stirred gently. Drop two cubes into each glass at the same moment and start the timer.
flow.say: Here come the cubes. Two in each glass, all at once, so the glasses get the same time. The timer starts now.
flow.kid: Pour water into each glass. A grown-up pours the hot water. Drop two cubes in each glass. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Hand-hot means as warm as you can comfortably touch, about 45 degrees. The kettle water is far too hot to touch, so keep glass C on the tray. Pour the hot water slowly into glass C, with a steel spoon standing in the glass. Stir the soap gently so it does not foam over. If you have a thermometer, write the water temperatures in the table.
flow.context: In this step, you fill the four glasses and start the test.

flow.do: Hold a sheet of white paper behind each glass at 5, 10 and 20 minutes. Give each glass a colour score from 0 to 5. Write the scores in the table. Do not stir.
flow.say: Look at each glass against the white paper. Give it a score from 0 for clear to 5 for deep red. Which glass changes first? What do you see?
flow.kid: Look at each glass against white paper. Score its colour from 0 to 5. Do this three times.

ask.q: Which glass changed first, and which has not changed at all?
good: The hot glass changed first.
The cold glass is still clear.

flow.parent: Hot water should turn red within minutes. Soap is usually slower and fainter than heat, and dish soaps differ, so D may be only pinkish at 20 minutes. Warm water may give a faint pink. Cold water usually stays clear or very faintly pink. If even the hot glass stays pale, the beetroot is probably old or has been cooked: use a fresh firm one and thinner cubes. Otherwise, if your results differ, write them down as they are. That is a result too. With two to four children, one child turns the labels away and scores the glasses without knowing which is which, then the others check the labels and compare. If you are alone, a grown-up shuffles the glasses for you. Each child can make a guess for one glass of their own.
flow.wait: Leave the glasses for 20 minutes in total.
flow.context: In this step, you watch the glasses and score their colour three times.

flow.do: Lift the cubes out of each glass with a spoon. Look at the colour of each cube. Write what you see in the last column of the table.
flow.say: Now lift out the cubes. What colour is a cube from the hot glass? What colour is a cube from the cold glass? What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Lift out one cube from each glass. Look at its colour. Is it as red as before?
flow.parent: The cube from the hot glass should be pale. The red has left it and gone into the water. The cube from the cold glass should still be deep red. So the red is moved, not made.

check.q: Why is the water in glass C red, and the cube from glass C pale?
options: The hot water made new red colour.
The heat broke the cell skins and the red colour spilled out of the cells.
The cube soaked up the water and lost its colour.
check.why: The red is stored inside the cells. Heat breaks the fatty skin of the cell and the skin of the vacuole inside her. The red then leaves into the water. A wrong pick of the first kind means the colour was thought to appear from nothing. The cube losing its red shows the colour moved out. Try the cold glass again to see no colour move.

flow.context: This step checks the cubes, to see where the red went.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain the membrane. Draw the four glasses with the colours you saw.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Draw the four glasses.
flow.parent: After they have said what they saw, explain. Each beetroot cell holds a store of red pigment in a bag called a vacuole. A fatty skin, the membrane, wraps both the bag and the cell. A whole skin lets the red stay in. Heat melts the fat of the skin and bends the proteins that sit in it. Soap dissolves fat, so it opens the skin too. Cold leaves the skin whole. A membrane only holds if it is whole and alive. If the child is curious, try a frozen and thawed cube. Ice crystals tear the skins, so it spills red too.
flow.think: You also freeze a cube for an hour and then let it thaw in cold water. Do you think it will spill red? Why?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Beetroot Test. You say what you found and why.

experiments.title: Banana DNA: can you pull the recipe book out of a cell?
experiments.question: Can you see DNA with your own eyes if you break open the cells of a banana?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will you see anything, and what will it look like? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The test glass holds the banana liquid. The check glass holds plain warm water with soap and salt but no banana, filled to the same depth. Both get the same amount of cold alcohol. If strands appear only where the banana is, the strands came from the banana.
results_table: What I saw at the top after 5 minutes

materials.item: half a ripe banana (or 4 ripe strawberries)
half a cup of warm tap water
a quarter teaspoon of salt
1 teaspoon of clear liquid dish soap
a fork and a bowl
a coffee filter or a clean thin cotton cloth, and a funnel or a tea strainer
2 tall clear glasses or small narrow jars
isopropyl alcohol (90 percent or stronger), about 100 millilitres for each glass, chilled in the freezer for at least an hour
a toothpick or a clean bamboo skewer

experiments.safety: A grown-up handles the rubbing alcohol. It burns easily, so keep it away from the stove and any flame. It is poisonous, so nobody tastes it or the banana mixture. Wash hands afterwards. Do not leave the glasses where a younger child can reach them. Work near an open window, and check that nobody is allergic to banana or strawberry.
experiments.record: Write what you saw at the top layer after 5 minutes, in both glasses. Draw the tall glass with its layers: banana liquid at the bottom, alcohol on top, and the white strands between.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you break open banana cells and pull out the DNA from their nuclei. You use soap, salt and cold alcohol.

setup.art: A fork mashing half a ripe banana in a bowl with warm water and a pinch of salt.
setup.caption: 1. Mash the banana with warm water and a pinch of salt.

setup.art: A spoon slowly stirring a teaspoon of dish soap into the banana mixture, with no foam on top.
setup.caption: 2. Add soap and stir slowly for three minutes, without making foam.

setup.art: The banana mixture being poured through a coffee filter into a tall clear glass.
setup.caption: 3. Strain the mixture through a coffee filter or a clean cloth into a tall glass.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring cold rubbing alcohol slowly down the side of a tilted glass, making a clear layer on top.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up tilts the glass and pours cold alcohol slowly down the side.

setup.art: White cloudy strands rising from the boundary between the banana liquid and the alcohol, and a toothpick lifting them.
setup.caption: 5. After a few minutes, white strands rise. Lift them with a toothpick.

flow.do: Put the bottle of rubbing alcohol in the freezer an hour before you start. Set out everything on a tray. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Every cell in a banana has a nucleus with DNA. Will we see any of it with our eyes? What do you think it will look like? Why?
flow.kid: Is there DNA in a banana? Can you see it? What would it look like?

ask.q: What do you think DNA looks like when it is out of the cell?
good: Tiny thin threads.
Like a white cloud.
We cannot see it.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Many children expect a tiny ladder. Real DNA from many cells together looks like white stringy cloud.
flow.context: This is the first step of Banana DNA. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Mash half a ripe banana with a fork in a bowl until it is smooth like paste. Add half a cup of warm water and a quarter teaspoon of salt. Stir.
flow.say: Mashing breaks the banana into small pieces, so the soap can reach the cells. The salt will help the DNA clump together later.
flow.kid: Mash the banana until it is smooth. Add warm water and salt. Stir.
flow.parent: Warm water from the tap is fine, not hot. The smoother the paste, the more cells are opened. A ripe banana works best. With two to four children, each child can mash a quarter banana in their own cup and make their own glass, and the grown-up pours the alcohol for each. Alone, make one banana glass and one check glass.
flow.context: In this step, you mash the banana with warm water and salt.

flow.do: Add one teaspoon of dish soap. Stir slowly for three minutes. Try not to make foam. Leave it for five minutes.
flow.say: The soap breaks the fatty skins around the cells and around the nuclei. Remember the beetroot test. Stir gently, because foam traps the DNA.
flow.kid: Add the soap. Stir slowly for three minutes. Do not make foam.

ask.q: What did soap do to the beetroot cells?
good: It opened the skin and the red came out.

flow.parent: This connects to the beetroot test. Soap dissolves the fatty membranes of the cells and the nuclei, so the DNA is set free. It helps to stand the cup in a bowl of hot tap water for ten minutes while it sits, but not water that is too hot to touch.
flow.context: This step breaks open the cells with soap.

flow.do: Pour the mixture through a coffee filter or a clean thin cloth into a tall glass. Fill the glass about one third full. Pour a second small glass with water, soap and salt but no banana, as a check.
flow.say: The filter catches the lumps. The clear liquid has the DNA in it, but it is too thin to see. We make a check glass with no banana too.
flow.kid: Strain the mixture into a tall glass. Make a check glass with no banana.
flow.parent: Squeeze the filter gently, but do not tear it. Make the check glass the same depth as the banana glass.
flow.context: In this step, you strain the mixture and make a check glass.

flow.do: A grown-up tilts the glass. Slowly pour cold alcohol down the side, until it makes a layer as deep as the banana liquid. Do not stir. Leave it for five minutes. Watch the line between the layers.
flow.say: Slowly now. The alcohol floats on top. DNA does not dissolve in alcohol. Watch the line between the two layers. What do you see?
flow.kid: A grown-up pours cold alcohol down the side. Watch the line between the layers.

ask.q: What do you see at the line between the layers?
good: White cloudy strands.
Stringy stuff rising up.

flow.parent: If nothing shows after five minutes, wait five more. If it is still nothing, the alcohol may have been too warm or too weak (70 percent works poorly), or the mixture was stirred too hard. Pour more cold alcohol and try again with a new glass. A clear line with a white cloud on it is success. Banana gives a modest cloud, not a thick rope, so a few small white threads count. Strawberries give more.
flow.wait: Leave the glass still for five minutes.
flow.context: In this step, you add cold alcohol and wait for the DNA.

flow.do: Twirl a toothpick in the white strands and lift them out. Look at what you have. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Twirl the toothpick slowly. That white stringy stuff is DNA, mixed with a few other things, from millions of banana nuclei. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Twirl a toothpick in the strands. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: The strands are DNA from many cells, mixed with some protein. A single DNA molecule is too thin to see. Millions together make a cloud. The child can keep the toothpick in a jar of alcohol for days.

check.q: Why did the soap come before the alcohol?
options: Soap breaks the cell and nucleus skins, so the DNA comes out into the liquid.
check.why: The DNA is locked inside nuclei, behind two skins. Soap dissolves the fat of the skins and frees it. A pick of the first kind confuses soap with cold. Try mixing without soap, and see that little white appears.

flow.context: This is the last step of Banana DNA. You lift the DNA out and say what you found.

experiments.title: Warm Sprouts: do living seeds make heat?
experiments.question: Is a flask of sprouting moong warmer than a flask of boiled moong after a night?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the sprouts be warmer, colder or the same as the boiled seeds? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both flasks get the same amount of moong, the same container, the same towel wrapping, and the same place in the house. Only one thing differs: the seeds in one flask are alive, and the seeds in the other are not.

materials.item: 2 cups of whole green moong

2 identical vacuum (thermos) flasks, wide-mouth if you can, about 400 to 500 millilitres each. A tea or water flask from the kitchen will do. A plain steel dabba loses heat too fast and may show no difference.
2 thermometers, or one thermometer used one after the other
2 towels and a cardboard box to hold both
a pan and a stove (for the grown-up)
a sieve

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the moong. Do not eat any seeds from the flasks, because the boiled ones can go bad and smell sour. Wash the flasks well afterwards. Check that nobody is allergic to moong. Hot water and the stove are for the grown-up only. Keep the flasks in a safe place away from pets.

schedule.what: Soak 2 cups of moong in plenty of water for 8 hours or overnight.
Drain the moong. A grown-up boils half of it for 10 minutes and cools it. Fill both flasks to the top. Take the start temperature.
Measure both flasks again in the morning and compare.

experiments.record: Write both temperatures at the start and the next morning. Work out the difference. Write whether the flask smells different. Draw a thermometer for each flask.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out whether living seeds make heat. You compare sprouting moong with boiled moong, which can no longer sprout.

setup.art: A bowl of green moong soaking in water on a kitchen counter at night.
setup.caption: 1. Soak two cups of moong in water overnight.

setup.art: A pan of boiled moong cooling next to a bowl of soaked, raw moong.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up boils half of the soaked moong. Let it cool.

setup.art: Two steel flasks side by side, each filled with moong, with a probe thermometer pushed into the seeds of each.
setup.caption: 3. Fill two flasks to the top. Push a thermometer into the seeds of each.

setup.art: Both flasks wrapped in towels and standing in a cardboard box in a quiet corner.
setup.caption: 4. Wrap both in towels. Put them in a box in a quiet corner.

flow.do: On the evening before, soak two cups of moong in plenty of water for 8 hours or overnight. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both down.
flow.say: Seeds are alive. When wet, they wake up. Will a flask of waking seeds be warmer than a flask of boiled seeds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Soak the moong overnight. Guess which flask will be warmer, and why.

ask.q: Do you think living seeds make heat? Why?
good: Yes, because they are doing things.
No, because seeds just sit there.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good.
flow.wait: Leave the moong to soak overnight.
flow.context: This is the first step of Warm Sprouts. You soak the seeds and guess.

flow.do: Drain the moong in a sieve. A grown-up boils half of it for ten minutes, then drains and cools it to room temperature. The other half stays raw and wet.
flow.say: Boiling kills the seeds, so they cannot grow. Both piles are wet and the same amount. One is alive and one is not.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils half the moong. Cool it to room temperature. Keep the other half raw.
flow.parent: The boiled seeds must be fully cool before they go in the flask, or the start temperatures will not match.
flow.context: This step makes a living pile and a boiled pile of seeds.

flow.do: Fill both flasks right to the top with moong. Push a thermometer into the middle of the seeds in each, and set the lid on loosely. Write both starting temperatures. Wrap both flasks in towels and set them in a box in a quiet corner.
flow.say: Same container, same amount, same towel, same corner. What are the temperatures now? Write them down.
flow.kid: Fill both flasks. Put in thermometers. Write the starting temperatures. Wrap them in towels.
flow.parent: Keep the lids loose, because the sprouts make carbon dioxide. A full flask has little air to carry the heat away. If the thermometer cannot stay in with the lid on, read the start temperature, close the flask, and read it again at the end by opening the lid and pushing the thermometer in at once. With two to four children, each child owns one job: filler, thermometer reader, writer and timekeeper, and swaps for the next reading. Everyone makes a guess first. If you only have one thermometer, read one flask and then the other, with no delay. The start temperatures should be within half a degree of each other.
flow.context: In this step, you fill and wrap the flasks, and take the first temperatures.

flow.do: The next morning, open each flask and read the temperature at once. Write the numbers. Work out the difference. Smell each flask.
flow.say: Open the flasks and read the temperatures quickly. Which is warmer? By how much? What do the seeds smell like?
flow.kid: Read both temperatures at once. Which flask is warmer? Smell each one.

ask.q: Which flask is warmer, and by how much?
good: The sprouting one is warmer by about a degree.

flow.parent: In a good vacuum flask, the sprouts are typically warmer by about half a degree to two degrees. Seeds make only a little heat, so in a plain dabba the difference may be too small to see, or nothing. If both flasks warmed, the boiled seeds may carry microbes that also make heat. That is a real effect, so say so. If the difference is nothing, say so and try again with more seeds in a better flask.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the flasks the next morning.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain. Pour the seeds into the compost or bin.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: Waking seeds release the energy stored in their sugar and starch, using oxygen, in their mitochondria. Some energy goes into building the new sprout, and some leaves as heat. Boiled seeds cannot do this, though germs in them can make a little heat too, so the difference is small. It is the same reason you warm up when you run.
flow.think: Where did the heat come from, if nobody lit a fire?

check.q: Why was the boiled flask a check on the test?
options: It showed what the flask does when the seeds are not alive.
It showed that boiled seeds make more heat.
It made the sprouts grow faster.
check.why: Both flasks are the same in everything but one thing. If the living seeds are warmer, the difference comes from being alive. A wrong pick of the second kind means the check was mistaken for the test.

flow.context: This is the last step of Warm Sprouts. You say what you found and why.

activities.title: The Copy Walk: from recipe book to bead necklace

materials.item: a strip of paper and 3 pens (red, blue and yellow)
a sticky note or a small slip of paper
4 kinds of dry grain or pulse in small bowls: chana, rice, moong and rajma (or four colours of beads)
a steel plate for the nucleus and a second plate for the ribosome

activities.safety: Dry grains are small. Keep them away from toddlers, and nobody puts them in the mouth, nose or ears. If a child is allergic to any pulse, use coloured paper bits or beads instead.
activities.record: Draw the recipe dots, the messenger copy, and the necklace you built each time. Write what changed when the dots changed.
activities.context: In this activity, you act out how a cell copies a recipe from her DNA and builds a protein, using coloured dots and four kinds of grain.

setup.art: A paper strip with eight dots in red, red, blue, yellow, yellow, red, blue, blue lying on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. The recipe book: eight coloured dots on a strip, on the nucleus plate.

setup.art: A hand copying the dots onto a sticky note, with the strip staying on its plate.
setup.caption: 2. Copy the dots onto a sticky note. The book stays on its plate.

setup.art: A child reading pairs of dots from the sticky note and picking grains into a row on the ribosome plate.
setup.caption: 3. At the ribosome plate, read two dots at a time and pick a grain.

flow.do: Draw eight dots on the paper strip in this order: red, red, blue, yellow, yellow, red, blue, blue. Put the strip on the steel plate. Then write the code on another paper. RR, RB and YY mean chana. RY and YR mean rice. BR and BB mean moong. BY and YB mean rajma.
flow.say: This strip is the recipe book in the nucleus. It must never leave the plate. Here is the code. Two dots in a row make one word, and each word means one grain.
flow.kid: Draw the eight dots. Put the strip on the plate. Write the code on a paper.
flow.parent: Real cells read three letters at a time, with four letters, so there are 64 words. We use two dots and three colours, so there are 9 words. Note that three different words mean chana. The real code also has several words for the same block.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Copy Walk. You make the recipe book and the code.

flow.do: Copy the dots onto the sticky note in the same order. This is the messenger copy. Carry it to the ribosome plate. The strip stays on its plate.
flow.say: A cell does not take the book out. She copies one recipe and sends the copy out. Copy the dots, and walk the copy to the ribosome.
flow.kid: Copy the dots onto the note. Walk it to the other plate. The book stays.

ask.q: Why do you think the cell copies the recipe and keeps the book?
good: So the book does not get lost or damaged.
So the book can be used again.

flow.context: In this step, you make the messenger copy and carry it to the ribosome.

flow.do: At the ribosome plate, read the note two dots at a time. Use the code to pick a grain for each pair. Line up the grains in order.
flow.say: You are the ribosome now. Read two dots, pick a grain. What is your necklace? It should have four grains.
flow.kid: Read two dots. Pick a grain. Do it four times. Line them up.
flow.parent: The right answer is chana, rajma, rice, moong. Check the pairs RR, BY, YR and BB against the code. With two to four children, one guards the book on the nucleus plate, one copies the note, and one is the ribosome. Swap parts, and let the guard draw a new strip of eight dots for the next round. Alone, play all three parts and let a grown-up draw the new strip.
flow.context: In this step, you act as the ribosome and build the protein.

flow.do: Now make a mistake on purpose. First, change the second dot of the first word from red to blue. Copy, read and build again. Then change the first dot of the first word from red to yellow. Copy, read and build again. Compare the three necklaces.
flow.say: A cell sometimes copies a letter wrongly. What happens to the necklace when one dot changes? Try both.
flow.kid: Change one dot. Build again. Then change a different dot. Compare the necklaces.

ask.q: Which change altered the necklace, and which did not?
good: Changing the first dot gave a rice grain instead of chana.
Changing the second dot made no difference.

flow.parent: Red-blue (RB) still means chana, so the first change makes no difference. Yellow-red (YR) means rice, so the second change swaps one grain. In real cells, a single changed letter can make no difference, or can change one building block, and sometimes that change causes a disease such as sickle cell anaemia.

check.q: When one letter in a recipe changes, what can happen?
options: Nothing, or one building block changes, depending on the change.
The cell makes a new kind of grain.
check.why: Because several words can mean the same block, some changes make no difference. Other changes swap one block, and that can change the shape and job of the protein. A wrong pick of the first kind suggests every change is harmful. Try the two changes above again.

flow.context: This step shows what a single changed letter can do.

activities.title: Power Cards: which cells need the most mitochondria?

materials.item: 5 small slips of paper and a pencil (a set for each child)
a table or the floor to lay them out

activities.record: Write your first order, and then the true order. Mark each place where you were surprised.
activities.context: In this activity, you guess which cells have the most mitochondria, then check the true order and think about why.

setup.art: Five slips of paper on a table, each with the name of a cell: red blood cell, sperm cell, liver cell, heart muscle cell, egg cell.
setup.caption: 1. Write one cell on each slip.

setup.art: The five slips laid out in a row from fewest to most mitochondria, as a child guessed.
setup.caption: 2. Lay them out from fewest mitochondria to most. Give a reason for each.

setup.art: The same slips rearranged into the true order, with the true numbers written under each.
setup.caption: 3. Move them into the true order. Write the numbers under each.

flow.do: Write these five cell names on five slips: red blood cell, sperm cell, liver cell, heart muscle cell, egg cell. Say that every cell is different in how much work she does.
flow.say: Mitochondria are the power stations. Which of these cells needs the most power? Which the least? Lay them in a row and tell me why.
flow.kid: Write five cell names on slips. Lay them from fewest mitochondria to most.

ask.q: Which cell do you think has the fewest, and why?
good: The red blood cell, because she only carries things.

ask.q: Which has the most, and why?
good: The heart cell, because she never rests.

flow.parent: Do not correct. Any order with a reason is a good start. With more than one child, each lays out their own row first. Compare the rows before you show the true order.
flow.context: This is the first step of Power Cards. You guess the order and give reasons.

flow.do: Show the true order. A red blood cell has none. A sperm cell has about 50 to 75, packed in a spiral behind the head. A liver cell has about 1,000 to 2,000. A heart muscle cell has thousands. An egg cell has about 100,000 or more. Move the slips into this order.
flow.say: Here is the true order. Which one surprised you? The egg cell is the biggest cell in the human body, and she has the most.
flow.kid: Move the slips into the true order. Which one surprised you?
flow.parent: Numbers vary from cell to cell and from person to person, so say 'about'. The egg is surprising. After fertilisation she divides many times using her own mitochondria, so she carries most of what the first cells of a baby will need. The sperm cell's mitochondria sit in a tight spiral behind the head and power her swimming.
flow.context: In this step, you check your order against the true order.

flow.do: Ask why the red blood cell has none. Then ask why the heart cell has so many. Write one sentence for each. Then work out roughly how many liver cells an egg cell equals in mitochondria, using about 100,000 and about 1,000.
flow.say: A red blood cell carries oxygen and keeps none for herself. Why would that help? And why does the heart cell have thousands?
flow.kid: Why does a red blood cell have none? Why does a heart cell have many?
flow.parent: A red blood cell carries oxygen and does not use it. If she had mitochondria, she would use up the oxygen she carries. Training does increase the number of mitochondria in muscle cells. The sum is 100,000 divided by 1,000, so about 100 liver cells. Say about, because the counts vary.
flow.think: If you trained for a race, would your muscle cells grow more mitochondria? Why?
flow.context: This step asks why the numbers differ.

activities.title: The Mother-Line Map: whose mitochondria do you carry?

materials.item: a large sheet of paper and pencils or crayons
an older relative to ask, in person or by phone

activities.record: Draw your mother-line map. Write each woman's name and where she lived, as far back as you can.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw the line of mothers behind you, because most of your mitochondria came to you through your mother's egg.

setup.art: A child at the bottom of a sheet of paper with an arrow upwards to a drawing of their mother, then her mother.
setup.caption: 1. Draw yourself and your mother. Draw an arrow from her to you.

setup.art: A chain of five women, each holding a small bean-shaped mitochondrion that is passed along the chain.
setup.caption: 2. Go back as far as you know. Draw a small bean beside each woman.

setup.art: A child counting the women on the chain and writing the number of years at the top.
setup.caption: 3. Count the women. About 25 years for each one gives the years.

flow.do: Draw yourself at the bottom of a large sheet. Draw your mother above you. Draw your mother's mother above her. Go back as far as you or an older relative can. Write each name and place. Draw a small bean-shaped mitochondrion beside each person. If you can, ask an elder where each woman was born, and mark the places on a rough sketch map of India.
flow.say: Your mitochondria came mostly from your mother's egg. Hers came from her mother. Let us draw the line. How far back can we go?
flow.kid: Draw yourself. Draw your mother above you. Add her mother. Go as far as you can.
flow.parent: If your family has adoption, loss or an unknown line, draw the line you know and stop there. That is part of the picture. Siblings share one mother-line, so they draw it together and each asks a different elder. Friends who are not related each draw their own and compare. Fathers and mothers both give DNA to the nucleus, but in most animals the mitochondria come from the egg.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Mother-Line Map. You draw the line of mothers.

flow.do: Count the women on your map. Multiply by 25 years for each one to estimate how many years the line goes back. Write it on top.
flow.say: Count the women. Each one is about 25 years. How many years back does your line go?
flow.kid: Count the women. Multiply by 25. How many years is that?
flow.parent: For example, 8 women times 25 years is 200 years. This is a rough estimate. If you have no names, pick a number, such as 10, and calculate.
flow.context: In this step, you count the women and estimate the years.

flow.do: Tell your child how far back the line of mothers goes in total. Ask what they notice. Then ask who in the line gets to pass on mitochondria. Boys receive them but, in most animals, do not pass them on.
flow.say: Every person alive has a line of mothers going back to the first cells. What do you think about that? Who passes the mitochondria on?
flow.kid: The line goes back to the first cells. What do you think about that?

ask.q: What do you think about a line of mothers going all the way back?
good: It is very long.
It goes back to before people.

flow.parent: Mitochondrial DNA is used by scientists to trace maternal lines. All living humans share a maternal ancestor, often called mitochondrial Eve, who lived roughly 150,000 to 200,000 years ago in Africa. She was not the only woman alive then, and other women's lines simply did not continue to the present through daughters only.
flow.context: This step ties the map to the story of the first cells.

projects.title: Cell City on a Tray: build the rooms and walk a protein through

materials.item: a large steel thali or tray
atta dough (colour it with turmeric, beetroot juice, spinach paste or a few drops of food colour) or modelling clay from a stationery shop, in five colours
dry lentils or sesame seeds for ribosomes
toothpicks and small paper flags
a small bowl for the vacuole and green dough for chloroplasts (for a plant cell)
a string or a thick rope of dough for the membrane
paper and pens for job cards

projects.safety: Dough is safe to touch. Do not eat the dough with the lentils mixed in. Wheat and sesame are common allergens, so use clay and lentils instead if anyone is allergic. Dry lentils and toothpicks are for older children only, and keep them away from toddlers.

schedule.what: Build the rooms and label them with job cards.
Walk a protein through the city and write three things the model gets wrong.

projects.record: Take a photo or draw the finished city with every room labelled. Write the path of a protein from the nucleus to the outside. Write three things the model gets wrong.
projects.context: In this project, you build a model of a cell on a tray, with the rooms from this unit, and walk a protein through it.

setup.art: A steel thali with a rope of dough around the rim as the membrane and a round dough ball in the middle with holes in it as the nucleus.
setup.caption: 1. Make the membrane with a dough rope. Make the nucleus with holes for pores.

setup.art: Bean-shaped dough mitochondria with folded paper inside, and lentil ribosomes scattered over folded dough strips.
setup.caption: 2. Make mitochondria, ribosomes, rough ER and Golgi from dough and lentils.

setup.art: Small paper flags on toothpicks stuck into each room, each flag naming a job.
setup.caption: 3. Stick a flag in each room with its job.

setup.art: A finger tracing a path from the nucleus through the ER and Golgi to the edge of the tray.
setup.caption: 4. Trace the path of a protein from the nucleus to the outside.

flow.do: Press a rope of dough around the rim of the tray for the membrane. Make a round nucleus and poke holes in it. Make five bean-shaped mitochondria. Make two small green ovals for chloroplasts if you build a plant cell.
flow.say: We are building a cell on a tray. The rope is the membrane. The ball with holes is the nucleus. The beans are mitochondria. What else will she need?
flow.kid: Make a dough rope for the membrane. Make a nucleus with holes. Make bean mitochondria.
flow.parent: Leave space for the rooms to be crowded. The picture is meant to be packed. Keep atta dough rooms in a closed box or under a damp cloth overnight, or they dry and crack. With two to four children, share one tray: each child makes some of the rooms, and on day two each takes a turn walking a protein through and saying what happens. Alone, expect the whole job to take the full hour.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cell City. You make the big rooms.

flow.do: Make the rough ER from folded strips of dough with lentils on them. Make a Golgi from a stack of curved strips. Make a lysosome from a small ball. Press a bowl in for the vacuole in a plant cell. Write a flag for each room, saying its job, and stick it in.
flow.say: Add the workshops. Lentils on the folded strips are ribosomes. The stack is the Golgi. Write a job on each flag.
flow.kid: Make the ER, Golgi and lysosome. Add lentils. Write a flag for each room.

ask.q: Where do the proteins go after the ribosome?
good: To the ER, then the Golgi, then out.

flow.context: In this step, you add the workshops and label every room.

flow.do: On day two, pick a protein to follow. Put a lentil at the nucleus. Move it through a pore, to a ribosome on the rough ER, along to the Golgi, and to the edge. Say what happens at each room. Then trace where oxygen and sugar enter and where the mitochondria use them.
flow.say: Today a protein travels through the city. Move your lentil from room to room. What happens at each one?
flow.kid: Move a lentil from the nucleus to the edge. Say what each room does.
flow.parent: The path is: copy leaves the nucleus through a pore, a ribosome on the rough ER builds the protein, the protein is folded in the ER, the Golgi labels it, a bubble carries it to the membrane. Oxygen and sugar come in through the membrane, and the mitochondria use them.
flow.wait: This step is for the second day.
flow.context: In this step, you walk a protein through the model.

flow.do: Ask your child to write three things the model gets wrong. For example, it stays still, it has a flat floor, and it shows only a few rooms. Look at the tray and compare.
flow.say: Our model sits still. A real cell never does. What else is different? Write three things the model gets wrong.
flow.kid: Write three things the model gets wrong. Is there a boss in the city?
flow.parent: Good answers: the real cell moves and jostles all the time, the rooms are crowded, there are millions of ribosomes, the cell has no single boss, the model is flat, and it is huge compared with the real thing. A real cell is usually only 10 to 30 micrometres wide.
flow.context: This is the last step of Cell City. You say where the model fails.

challenges.title: A Cell for the Job: share out twenty rooms
challenges.problem: You are designing a cell for a job, and you have only twenty room stickers to share among six kinds: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes and rough ER, Golgi, lysosomes, chloroplasts. The cell must work well. Your first job is a leg muscle cell in a runner.
constraints: Give every cell at least one nucleus sticker, except a red blood cell.
Explain every choice in one sentence.
Only a plant cell can have chloroplasts.
Use what you learned about the rooms.
materials: 20 small round stickers or dots drawn with a pen
general: A muscle cell: one nucleus, twelve mitochondria stickers, a few ribosomes and some Golgi, because she needs lots of power.
A leaf cell: some mitochondria, many chloroplasts, one nucleus, a few ribosomes.
A digestive gland cell: lots of ribosomes and rough ER and Golgi, some mitochondria, because she makes and posts a lot of protein.
creative: A cell for a bird that flies over the Himalaya, such as the bar-headed goose: more mitochondria stickers than a runner, and a note on why.
A cell for a cave animal with no light and very little food: very few mitochondria, and a reason.
A cell with no nucleus, like a red blood cell, with only room for oxygen: none of the six kinds of sticker, and a note on what she carries and how long she can live (about four months).
challenges.your_turn: Pick a job from your own day: a cell in your eye, your tongue, your hair root or your bone. Share out twenty stickers and explain each choice. Then ask someone else to guess the job from your stickers alone.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the rooms of a cell. You share out twenty stickers for a given job.

setup.art: A big circle on paper for a cell, with twenty small dots stuck in groups of different colours.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a cell. Stick twenty dots in groups for six kinds of rooms.

setup.art: A key at the side listing six colours and the names of the six rooms.
setup.caption: 2. Make a colour key. Write one reason for each group.

setup.art: Two cells side by side with different dot groups, labelled leg muscle and digestive gland.
setup.caption: 3. Make a second cell for a different job. Compare the two.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Draw a big circle for the cell. Make a key with six colours for the six rooms. Ask what a leg muscle cell does all day.
flow.say: You are designing a cell for a job with twenty stickers. What does a runner's leg muscle cell do? Which rooms will she need most?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Draw a big circle. Make a colour key for six rooms.

ask.q: What does a leg muscle cell need most?
good: Power, so mitochondria.
A way to get oxygen.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Cell for the Job. You read the problem and set up.

flow.do: Share out twenty dots among the rooms for the muscle cell. Write one sentence of reason for each group. Check that you used all twenty.
flow.say: Put your twenty dots in the cell. Why that many mitochondria? Why that many ribosomes?
flow.kid: Stick twenty dots. Write a reason for each group of dots.
flow.parent: There is no single right answer. A strong design gives most dots to mitochondria and has a reason for every group.
flow.context: In this step, you design the muscle cell and give your reasons.

flow.do: Design a second cell for a different job, such as a leaf cell or a digestive gland cell. Share out twenty dots again. Compare the two cells and say what changed.
flow.say: Now a leaf cell, or a cell in your stomach wall. Twenty dots again. What changes from the muscle cell?
flow.kid: Design a second cell for another job. Compare it with the first.

ask.q: What did you change between the two cells, and why?
good: More chloroplasts for the leaf.
More ribosomes and Golgi for the gland cell.

flow.context: In this step, you make a second cell and compare the two.

flow.do: Now do the 'your turn' job from your own day. Ask someone to guess the job from your dots alone. Write what they guessed and why.
flow.say: Pick a cell from your own body. Share out twenty dots. Let someone guess the job from the dots.
flow.kid: Pick a cell from your body. Stick twenty dots. Let someone guess its job.
flow.parent: Real cells have many more rooms than twenty, and they are not set by sticker. The point is that the number of each room follows the job.
flow.think: If the same twenty dots were used in every cell, would cells be different from each other?
flow.context: This is the last step of A Cell for the Job. You design a cell and test it on someone.

items.p: Which room of a cell releases energy from food, using oxygen?
opts: The nucleus
The mitochondrion
The Golgi body
items.why: Mitochondria release energy from sugar, using oxygen, and store it in ATP. The nucleus keeps the DNA, and the Golgi body labels and posts proteins. If you picked the nucleus, remember that the nucleus is where recipes are kept, not where energy is made.

items.p: What does a ribosome do?
opts: It stores the DNA
It reads a messenger copy and builds a protein
It digests swallowed germs
items.why: A ribosome reads a copy of one gene and joins building blocks in order to make a protein. The DNA is kept in the nucleus, and germs are digested in lysosomes.

items.p: The nucleus keeps the DNA inside and sends out copies of single genes.
items.why: True. Copies of single genes, called messenger RNA, leave through tiny doors in the nucleus. The DNA itself stays in.

items.p: Mitochondria release energy from food using ____.
items.why: Mitochondria need oxygen to release the most energy from sugar. That is why you breathe harder when you run.

items.p: Match each room to its job.
items.why: Each room has one main job, and the jobs fit together. Ribosomes build, the Golgi posts, mitochondria power, lysosomes recycle, and the nucleus keeps the recipes.

items.p: Sort each part by whether it is found only in plant cells or in both plant and animal cells.
items.why: Chloroplasts and the big central vacuole belong to plant cells. Mitochondria, nucleus, ribosomes and the Golgi body are found in both. Plants breathe with mitochondria, as animals do.

items.p: Put these steps in order for how a cell makes a protein.
a: A gene is copied into a messenger copy
The copy leaves the nucleus through a pore
Building blocks are joined in order
The chain folds into a protein
items.why: A cell copies the recipe first and keeps the book. The copy travels to a ribosome, which reads it and builds the chain. The chain folds into its shape last.

items.p: Beetroot cubes turn the water red in hot water but not in cold water. What is the best explanation?
opts: Heat makes new red colour
Heat breaks the cell skins, so the red leaves the cells
Cold water washes the red away
items.why: The red is stored inside the cells. A whole skin keeps it in. Heat melts the fatty skin, so the red spills. Cold leaves the skin whole.

items.p: Plant cells have chloroplasts and no mitochondria.
items.why: False. Plant cells have both. Chloroplasts make sugar in light, and mitochondria release energy from the sugar, day and night.

items.p: A friend says: 'The nucleus is the boss of the cell because she gives all the orders.' What would you tell your friend, using what you know about cells?
items.a: The nucleus keeps the recipes, but she does not give orders alone. Signals from the rest of the cell and from outside tell her which recipes to copy. A red blood cell has no nucleus and still works for months. Mitochondria even keep a little DNA of their own.
items.why: A strong answer says that the nucleus stores the recipes and that other parts and outside signals decide which recipe is used. It may give the red blood cell or the mitochondrial DNA as evidence.

items.p: Draw a cell with six rooms. Label each room and write its job in three words.
items.a: A cell with a membrane, a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, a Golgi body and a lysosome, each labelled with a short job.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the nucleus inside its own skin, bean-shaped mitochondria with a folded wall, and ribosomes as small dots. Small mistakes in shape do not matter. The jobs matter.

items.p: Which fact is the best evidence that mitochondria were once bacteria?
opts: They have their own ring of DNA and divide on their own
They are bean-shaped
They are found in animal cells
items.why: A ring of DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes and splitting in two are all things bacteria do. Shape alone is not enough evidence, and being in animal cells says nothing about where they came from.

items.p: A teacher says: 'A cell is just a tiny city.'

views.says: The city picture helps children remember that a cell has rooms with different jobs, like shops and power stations.
A real cell is always moving, very crowded, and has no mayor. The picture can make us think a cell is calm and orderly.
I would use the city picture to remember the rooms, and then add what it leaves out.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most, and what does the picture leave out?
items.a: Any view with a reason is good.
items.why: Both the teacher and the biologist are right about different things. A picture helps with the rooms and misleads about the movement and the lack of a boss.

items.p: Explain why a cell that works very hard has many mitochondria. Use the words energy, oxygen and ATP.
items.a: A hard-working cell spends a lot of energy. Mitochondria use oxygen to release energy from sugar and store it in ATP, and ATP is used up almost as fast as it is made. More mitochondria means more ATP every second.
items.why: A strong answer links hard work to a big spending of ATP and says that mitochondria make ATP from food and oxygen. Many mitochondria make more ATP at once.

items.p: A ribosome in a bacterium adds 20 building blocks to a protein every second. How long does it take to add 100 building blocks?
items.why: 100 divided by 20 is 5. A ribosome builds fast, and a cell has millions of them.

items.p: Why is the inner wall of a mitochondrion folded many times?
opts: The folds give more surface for the energy machines to sit on
The folds make the mitochondrion green
The folds let the mitochondrion hold more water
items.why: The machines that release energy sit in the inner wall. Folding gives a much larger wall in the same small room, so more machines can work. It is like folding a long towel into a small bucket.

items.p: Scientists put the nucleus of a frog's gut cell into an egg cell that had no nucleus of its own, and a tadpole grew. What does this show?
opts: Gut cells are really egg cells
The gut cell's nucleus still held the whole recipe
Eggs do not need a nucleus
items.why: A tadpole needs all the recipes, so the gut cell's nucleus must have held them all. The gut cell used only a few pages. The rest were still there.

items.p: Mitochondria divide in two inside a cell, much as bacteria do. Why is this a clue about their past?
opts: The cell cannot make a new mitochondrion from nothing, so each comes from an older one
They are bigger than bacteria
They are the same colour as bacteria
items.why: Only existing mitochondria make new ones, as only existing bacteria make new bacteria. This fits their having begun as bacteria. Size and colour are not clues.

items.p: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus and still lives for months.
items.why: True. A red blood cell carries oxygen for about four months with no nucleus. She uses proteins that were built before she lost her nucleus.

items.p: A ribosome reads a messenger copy ____ letters at a time.
items.why: Each three-letter word on the copy means one building block. The ribosome reads one word after another and adds the blocks in order.

items.p: Match each part to what it looks like.
pairs: a stack of flat curved bags
folded bags with ribosomes on them
a small round bag of strong juice
items.why: Each room's shape suits its job. A stack of flat bags is good for sorting, and the folds of the ER make room for many ribosomes.

items.p: Which beetroot test is the odd one out, and why? Cold water, hot water, soapy water, frozen then thawed.
items.a: Cold water, because the others all break the cell skins and the red spills. In cold water the skins stay whole.
items.why: Heat, soap and ice crystals break the skins. Cold water leaves them whole, so the red stays inside.

items.p: A person makes about their own body weight in ATP in a day. A girl weighs 30 kilograms. About how much ATP does she make in 10 days?
items.why: 30 kilograms a day times 10 days is 300 kilograms. She never holds that much at once. She uses ATP almost as fast as she makes it.

items.p: A gene has 900 letters. A ribosome reads it three letters at a time. How many building blocks will the protein have?
items.why: 900 divided by 3 is 300. Each three-letter word means one building block.

items.p: How could scientists tell whether a room of a cell began as a bacterium? Name two things they would look for.
items.a: They would look for a ring of DNA of its own, ribosomes like those of bacteria, and whether the room splits in two without help. They could also compare its gene letters with those of living bacteria.
items.why: A strong answer names signs of bacteria: a ring of DNA of its own, bacteria-like ribosomes, splitting in two without help, or gene letters that match bacteria.

items.p: Your muscle cells and your skin cells hold the same DNA. Explain how they can still be so different.
items.a: Each kind of cell switches on different genes. A muscle cell uses the muscle recipes and a skin cell uses the skin recipes. The switches are pressed by proteins and signals from inside and outside the cell.
items.why: A strong answer says the recipes are the same but different ones are used, and that signals and switch proteins decide which. It does not say the DNA is different.

items.p: Draw a mitochondrion with its two skins and the folds. Mark where food and oxygen go in and what comes out.
items.a: A bean shape with a double outline and a wavy inner wall. Arrows in for sugar and oxygen, and arrows out for ATP, carbon dioxide and water.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two skins, folds on the inner one, and the right things going in and out.

items.p: Put these steps in order for how a cell gets energy from sugar.
a: The sugar is split in the cytoplasm, releasing a little energy
The halves go into a mitochondrion
With oxygen, much more energy is released as ATP
items.why: The first split, without oxygen, gives only a little energy. The mitochondrion, with oxygen, gives about fifteen times more. Carbon dioxide is the waste.

items.p: A friend says: 'Genes are the boss of the body.'

views.says: Genes carry the information that builds every protein. Everything a body does starts with them, so they come first.
Genes sit unused until signals switch them on. The whole cell and its surroundings decide which genes are used.
Both matter. A change in a gene can cause illness, and food, exercise and stress change how genes are used.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing, and what evidence would change your mind?
items.a: Any view with a reason is good.
items.why: Scientists disagree about how to describe the relationship, and the evidence supports both a role for genes and a role for the whole cell.

items.p: Sort each statement by whether the city picture of a cell helps or misleads.
items: A mayor in the nucleus gives all orders
Finished goods are posted from one place to another
Everything stays still in its place
Power stations make energy for the whole city
Buildings stay where they were put
items.why: The picture is good for rooms, jobs and posting. It misleads about a boss and about stillness, because a cell has no mayor and everything in her moves.

quiz.p: Which room of a cell keeps the DNA?
opts: The mitochondrion
The nucleus
The lysosome
quiz.why: The nucleus keeps the DNA. Mitochondria release energy and lysosomes digest old parts.

quiz.p: Why do you breathe harder when you run?
opts: Your cells need more oxygen to release more energy
Your lungs get smaller
Your blood turns blue
quiz.why: Your mitochondria use oxygen to release energy for your muscles. More work needs more oxygen, so you breathe harder.
Yes. Plant cells have chloroplasts and mitochondria. Mitochondria release energy from sugar in the day and in the night.

quiz.p: In what order does a cell make a protein?
opts: Copy the gene, carry the copy, build the protein
Build the protein, copy the gene, carry the copy
Carry the book, build the protein, copy the gene
quiz.why: The nucleus keeps the book and sends out a copy. The copy goes to a ribosome, which builds the protein.

quiz.p: Beetroot cubes stay pale in cold water and spill red in hot water. What does this show?
opts: Whole cell skins hold the red in, and heat breaks them
Beetroot makes red in hot water
Cold water has no effect on anything
quiz.why: The red is stored inside whole cells. Heat melts the fat of the skins, so the red leaves. In cold water the skins stay whole.

quiz.p: A ____ reads a messenger copy and builds a protein.
quiz.why: A ribosome is the tiny machine that reads the copy and joins the building blocks.

quiz.p: Which fact shows that the nucleus is not the only part in charge of a cell?
opts: A red blood cell lives for months with no nucleus
Nuclei are round
Plant cells are bigger than animal cells
quiz.why: A red blood cell works for months without a nucleus. The nucleus keeps the recipes, but the whole cell does the work.

quiz.p: Mitochondria have a small piece of DNA of their own.
quiz.why: True. Human mitochondria have a ring of DNA 16,569 letters long with 37 genes. This is one clue that they began as bacteria.

quiz.p: What does the city picture of a cell leave out?
opts: That a cell is always moving and has no single boss
That a cell has rooms
That a cell has a skin
quiz.why: A city picture shows rooms with jobs, which is useful. It leaves out the constant motion and the lack of any single ruler.

quiz.p: Which room digests old parts and swallowed germs?
opts: The lysosome
The ribosome
The chloroplast
quiz.why: Lysosomes are small bags of strong juice. Ribosomes build proteins and chloroplasts catch light.

quiz.p: Which of these is still an open question?
opts: How the first cell with a nucleus and mitochondria began
Whether cells have a skin
Whether mitochondria use oxygen
quiz.why: Scientists agree that cells have skins and that mitochondria use oxygen. How the first complex cell began is still argued.

quiz.p: Muscle cells and skin cells hold the same DNA. Why are they different?
opts: They switch on different genes
Their DNA is different
Muscle cells have no nucleus
quiz.why: Each cell uses the recipes it needs. Gurdon's frog experiment showed that a grown-up cell still holds the whole book.

applications: Doctors test for diseases of the mitochondria in babies who tire very easily.
Many antibiotics work by blocking bacterial ribosomes and leaving ours alone.
Plant scientists breed crops with more efficient chloroplasts to grow more food.
Forensic scientists and historians use mitochondrial DNA to follow a mother's line back many generations.
Vaccines made with messenger RNA ask the body's ribosomes to build one harmless protein from a virus.
Athletes train to give their muscle cells more mitochondria and more blood vessels.
Cooks keep beetroot and other coloured vegetables from bleeding by not breaking the cells.
Cancer drugs aim at cells that copy their DNA fast.

open_questions.q: How did the first cell with a nucleus and mitochondria begin?
open_questions.why_open: No living cell has been found part-way between a bacterium and a cell with rooms, and the oldest evidence is two billion years old.

open_questions.q: How does a muscle cell stay a muscle cell for decades, when she holds a whole recipe book?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many switches, but not how all of them add up to a steady choice.

open_questions.q: Why do mitochondria keep a few genes of their own, when most moved to the nucleus?
open_questions.why_open: There are several ideas, but no single test has settled which is right.

open_questions.q: How did the first ribosomes begin?
open_questions.why_open: Ribosomes need proteins and proteins need ribosomes. Many scientists think RNA came first, but this is an idea.

open_questions.q: How does a cell know how big to grow?
open_questions.why_open: Some signals that control size are known, but cells of one kind in the same body can still differ in size.

open_questions.q: Is a cell more than the sum of her rooms?
open_questions.why_open: Biologists disagree on whether the whole cell has features that cannot be read from the parts.

maths.problem: A nucleus is 6 micrometres across. Its DNA, stretched out, is 2 metres long. How many times as long as the nucleus is the DNA? One metre is 1,000,000 micrometres.
maths.explain: Two metres is 2,000,000 micrometres. Dividing 2,000,000 by 6 gives about 333,000. So the DNA is about 333,000 times as long as the room it is kept in.
maths.context: In this unit you learn that a cell folds two metres of DNA into a nucleus a few micrometres wide.
maths.why_maths: Big numbers hide how astonishing a fact is, so dividing them shows how tightly the DNA is packed.

maths.problem: A liver cell has about 1,000 mitochondria. A human egg cell has at least 100,000. At least how many times as many mitochondria does the egg have? Why might an egg need so many?
maths.answer: At least 100 times as many, because the egg must power the first days of a new baby, before any other cells exist.
maths.explain: 100,000 divided by 1,000 is 100. The egg is large and, once it is fertilised, it divides with only the mitochondria it already holds.
maths.context: In the Power Cards activity you ranked cells by how many mitochondria they have.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two numbers by dividing tells you how many times larger one is, and then you can ask why.

maths.problem: In the beetroot test, a pupil scored the colour of the water on a scale of 0 to 5 after 20 minutes: cold water 0, warm water 1, hot water 5, soap water 4. How many points more is hot water than cold water, and which one is closest to the soap water?
maths.answer: 5 points more. Hot water (5) is closest to the soap water (4).
maths.explain: 5 minus 0 is 5. The soap score of 4 is one away from the hot score of 5, and four away from the cold score of 0.
maths.context: In the Beetroot Test you gave each glass a colour score from 0 to 5.
maths.why_maths: Comparing scores shows which treatments act alike, which hints that they break the cell skins in a similar way.

maths.problem: A ribosome in a bacterium adds about 20 building blocks every second. A small protein has 300 building blocks. About how long does it take one ribosome to build it?
maths.explain: 300 divided by 20 is 15. A cell has millions of ribosomes working together, so she can make millions of proteins in a few minutes.
maths.context: You learned that a ribosome builds a protein one building block at a time.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the size of a job by the speed of the worker gives the time, which shows how fast cells really build.

maths.problem: A red blood cell lives about 120 days. About how many red blood cells does your body replace in a year if it loses about the same number each day? A body makes about 2 million new red blood cells every second.
maths.explain: There are about 86,400 seconds in a day. 2 million times 86,400 is about 173 billion a day. Times 365 days is about 63 trillion a year.
maths.context: Red blood cells have no nucleus and last only about four months, so your body keeps making new ones.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a rate by time shows how much work a body does without you noticing.

maths.problem: In an imagined sprout heat test, the living sprouts reached 31 degrees after 12 hours and 33 degrees after 24 hours. The boiled seeds stayed at 28. How many degrees warmer were the living sprouts at the 12th hour and at the 24th hour?
maths.answer: 3 degrees warmer at 12 hours and 5 degrees warmer at 24 hours.
maths.explain: 31 minus 28 is 3. 33 minus 28 is 5. The difference grows, so the living seeds kept making heat.
maths.context: In the sprout heat test you compare living and boiled seeds over a day.
maths.why_maths: A difference between two readings shows what only the living seeds did, since both started the same.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1905 a Russian botanist named Konstantin Mereschkowski suggested that the green chloroplasts in plant cells were once free-living blue-green bacteria. Most scientists laughed. They thought the cell made all its rooms herself. In 1962 and 1963, other researchers found small amounts of DNA inside chloroplasts and mitochondria. Margit Nass found it in mitochondria. That was strange, because all the DNA was supposed to be in the nucleus. In 1967 a young American biologist named Lynn Margulis, then called Lynn Sagan, wrote a long paper arguing that both rooms had begun as bacteria. Her paper was turned down by about fifteen journals before one printed it. Then gene sequencing in the 1970s and 1980s showed that the rooms' DNA matched bacteria and not the nucleus. The idea that sounded foolish is now in every school book.
how_we_found_out.who: Konstantin Mereschkowski, Margit Nass, Lynn Margulis and later gene sequencers such as Carl Woese
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most scientists thought a cell built all her own rooms from the inside, and that all of the cell's DNA was in the nucleus. The small DNA rings found in mitochondria and chloroplasts, and later the gene sequences, showed that these two rooms had come from outside.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet cooked or tested at home. Beetroot Test: use fresh, firm raw beetroot and rinse the cubes well. The hot glass should turn red within minutes, soap in 10 to 20 minutes, warm water faintly, and cold water almost not at all. The colour scores in the maths question are an example, not measured. Banana DNA: the alcohol must be cold and 90 percent or stronger. With 70 percent alcohol the strands are thin or missing. Stir gently, because foam hides the result. If nothing shows, try again with fresh alcohol. Warm Sprouts: a difference of one to three degrees is typical in a good steel flask. A weak flask can give less. The boiled seeds also carry microbes that make a little heat, so a small difference is a fair result. The readings in the maths question are imagined. Copy Walk: the code uses two dots and three colours so a child can follow it. Real cells read three letters from four. Power Cards and the other numbers (mitochondria per cell, ATP in a day, 16,569 letters, 20 amino acids a second for a bacterial ribosome) are rounded figures to verify against a current cell biology text before the unit is finalised.
